exercise_group.instruction: Find the inverses of the matrices in Exercises ﻿1–4.

problem.paragraph: $$\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ - 7 & - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & - 2 \\ 7 & - 4 \end{bmatrix}$$
Verify that the inverse you found in Exercise 1 is correct.
Verify that the inverse you found in Exercise 2 is correct.
Use the inverse found in Exercise 1 to solve the system $$8 x_{1} & + & 3 x_{2} & = & 2 5 x_{1} & + & 2 x_{2} & = & - 1$$
Use the inverse found in Exercise 2 to solve the system $$3 x_{1} & + & x_{2} & = & - 2 7 x_{1} & + & 2 x_{2} & = & 3$$

Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 12 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{b}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{b}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{b}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}_{4} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ ﻿.

list.item: Find $$A^{- 1}$$ , and use it to solve the four equations $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}_{2}$$ , $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}_{3}$$ , $$A \textbf{x} = \textbf{b}_{4}$$

The four equations in part (a) can be solved by the same set of row operations, since the coefficient matrix is the same in each case. Solve the four equations in part (a) by row reducing the augmented matrix $$\begin{bmatrix} A & \textbf{b}_{1} & \textbf{b}_{2} & \textbf{b}_{3} & \textbf{b}_{4} \end{bmatrix}$$ ﻿

problem.paragraph: Use matrix algebra to show that if $$A$$ is invertible and $$D$$ satisfies $$AD = I$$ , then $$D = A^{- 1}$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 11–20, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) In order for a matrix $$B$$ to be the inverse of $$A$$ , both equations $$AB = I$$ and $$BA = I$$ must be true.
(T/F) A product of invertible $$n \times n$$ matrices is invertible, and the inverse of the product is the product of their inverses in the same order.
(T/F) If $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$n \times n$$ and invertible, then $$A^{- 1}B^{- 1}$$ is the inverse of $$AB$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$A$$ is invertible, then the inverse of $$A^{- 1}$$ is $$A$$ itself.
(T/F) If $$A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$ab - cd \neq 0$$ , then $$A$$ is invertible.
(T/F) If $$A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$ad = bc$$ , then $$A$$ is not invertible.
(T/F) If $$A$$ is an invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix, then the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is consistent for each $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿
(T/F) If $$A$$ can be row reduced to the identity matrix, then $$A$$ must be invertible.
(T/F) Each elementary matrix is invertible.
(T/F) If $$A$$ is invertible, then the elementary row operations that reduce $$A$$ to the identity $$I_{n}$$ also reduce $$A^{- 1}$$ to $$I_{n}$$ .﻿
Let $$A$$ be an invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix, and let $$B$$ be an $$n \times p$$ matrix. Show that the equation $$AX = B$$ has a unique solution $$A^{- 1}B$$ .﻿

Let $$A$$ be an invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix, and let $$B$$ be an $$n \times p$$ matrix. Explain why $$A^{- 1}B$$ can be computed by row reduction: $$\left. \text{If [} AB] \right.\sim\left. \cdots \right.\sim[IX], \text{then} X = A^{- 1}B.$$ If $$A$$ is larger than $$2 \times 2$$ , then row reduction of $$\lbrack A B\rbrack$$ is much faster than computing both $$A^{- 1}$$ and $$A^{- 1}B$$ .﻿
Suppose $$AB = AC$$ , where $$B$$ and $$C$$ are $$n \times p$$ matrices and $$A$$ is invertible. Show that $$B = C$$ . Is this true, in general, when $$A$$ is not invertible?
Suppose $$(B - C)D = 0$$ , where $$B$$ and $$C$$ are $$m \times n$$ matrices and $$D$$ is invertible. Show that $$B = C$$ .﻿

Suppose $$A$$ , $$B$$ , and $$C$$ are invertible $$n \times n$$ matrices. Show that $$ABC$$ is also invertible by producing a matrix $$D$$ such that $$\left( {ABC} \right)D = I$$ and $$D\left( {ABC} \right) = I$$ .﻿
Suppose $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$n \times n$$ , $$B$$ is invertible, and $$AB$$ is invertible. Show that $$A$$ is invertible. [Hint: Let $$C = AB$$ , and solve this equation for $$A$$ .]
Solve the equation $$AB = BC$$ for $$A$$ , assuming that $$A$$ , $$B$$ , and $$C$$ are square and $$B$$ is invertible.
Suppose $$P$$ is invertible and $$A = PBP^{- 1}$$ . Solve for $$B$$ in terms of $$A$$ .﻿
If $$A$$ , $$B$$ , and $$C$$ are $$n \times n$$ invertible matrices, does the equation $$C^{- 1}(A + X)B^{- 1} = I_{n}$$ have a solution, $$X$$ ? If so, find it.

Explain why the columns of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ are linearly independent when $$A$$ is invertible.
Explain why the columns of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ when $$A$$ is invertible. [Hint: Review Theorem 4 in Section 1.4.]

Suppose $$A$$ is $$n \times n$$ and the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has only the trivial solution. Explain why $$A$$ has $$n$$ pivot columns and $$A$$ is row equivalent to $$I_{n}$$ . By Theorem 7, this shows that $$A$$ must be invertible. (This exercise and Exercise 34 will be cited in Section 2.3.)

Suppose $$A$$ is $$n \times n$$ and the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has a solution for each $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Explain why $$A$$ must be invertible. [Hint: Is $$A$$ row equivalent to $$I_{n}$$ ?]

problem.paragraph: Show that if $$ad - bc = 0$$ , then the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has more than one solution. Why does this imply that $$A$$ is not invertible? [Hint: First, consider $$a = b = 0$$ . Then, if $$a$$ and $$b$$ are not both zero, consider the vector $$\textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} {- b} \\ a \end{bmatrix}$$ .]﻿
Show that if $$ad - bc \neq 0$$ , the formula for $$A^{- 1}$$ works.

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 37 and 38 prove special cases of the facts about elementary matrices stated in the box following Example 5. Here $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix and $$I = I_{3}$$ ﻿. (A general proof would require slightly more notation.)

list.item: Use equation (1) from Section 2.1 to show that $$\text{r} \text{o} \text{w} _{i}(A) = \text{r} \text{o} \text{w} _{i}(I) \cdot A$$ , for $$i = 1,2,3$$ .﻿
Show that if rows $$1$$ and $$2$$ of $$A$$ are interchanged, then the result may be written as $$EA$$ , where $$E$$ is an elementary matrix formed by interchanging rows $$1$$ and $$2$$ of $$I$$ .﻿
Show that if row $$3$$ of $$A$$ is multiplied by $$5$$ , then the result may be written as $$EA$$ , where $$E$$ is formed by multiplying row $$3$$ of $$I$$ by $$5$$ .

problem.paragraph: Show that if row $$3$$ of $$A$$ is replaced by $$\text{r} \text{o} \text{w} _{3}(A) - 4 \text{r} \text{o} \text{w} _{1}(A)$$ , the result is $$EA$$ , where $$E$$ is formed from $$I$$ by replacing $${ \text{r} \text{o} } \text{w} _{3}(I)$$ by $$\text{r} \text{o} \text{w} _{3}(I) - 4 \text{r} \text{o} \text{w} _{1}(I)$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: Find the inverses of the matrices in Exercises 39–42, if they exist. Use the algorithm introduced in this section.

problem.paragraph: $$\left[\right. 1 & 2 4 & 7 \left]\right.$$
$$\left[\right. 5 & 10 4 & 7 \left]\right.$$

Use the algorithm from this section to find the inverses of $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .$$
Let $$A$$ be the corresponding $$n \times n$$ matrix, and let $$B$$ be its inverse. Guess the form of $$B$$ , and then prove that $$A B = I$$ and $$BA = I$$ .﻿

Repeat the strategy of Exercise 43 to guess the inverse of $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 & & 0 \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & n \end{bmatrix}$$ . Prove that your guess is correct.
Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} {- 2} & {- 7} & {- 9} \\ 2 & 5 & 6 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find the third column of $$A^{- 1}$$ without computing the other columns.

Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Construct a $$2 \times 3$$ matrix $$C$$ (by trial and error) using only $$1$$ , $$- 1$$ , and $$0$$ as entries, such that $$CA = I_{2}$$ Compute $$AC$$ and note that $$AC \neq I_{3}$$ .﻿

Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Construct a $$4 \times 2$$ matrix $$D$$ using only $$1$$ and $$0$$ as entries, such that $$AD = I_{2}$$ . Is it possible that $$CA = I_{4}$$ for some $$4 \times 2$$ matrix $$C$$ ? Why or why not?

Let $$D = \begin{bmatrix} .005 & .002 & .001 \\ .002 & .004 & .002 \\ .001 & .002 & .005 \end{bmatrix}$$ be a flexibility matrix, with flexibility measured in inches per pound. Suppose that forces of $$30$$ , $$50$$ , and $$20 \text{lb}$$ are applied at points $$1$$ , $$2$$ , and $$3$$ , respectively, in Figure 1 of Example 3. Find the corresponding deflections.

[T] Compute the stiffness matrix $$D^{- 1}$$ for $$D$$ in Exercise 49. List the forces needed to produce a deflection of $$.04 \text{in}$$ . at point $$3$$ , with zero deflections at the other points.

[T] Let $$D = \begin{bmatrix} .0040 & .0030 & .0010 & .0005 \\ .0030 & .0050 & .0030 & .0010 \\ .0010 & .0030 & .0050 & .0030 \\ .0005 & .0010 & .0030 & .0040 \end{bmatrix}$$ be a flexibility matrix for an elastic beam with four points at which force is applied. Units are centimeters per newton of force. Measurements at the four points show deflections of $$.08$$ , $$.12$$ , $$.16$$ , and $$.12 \text{cm}$$ . Determine the forces at the four points.

[T] With $$D$$ as in Exercise 51, determine the forces that produce a deflection of $$.24 \text{cm}$$ at the second point on the beam, with zero deflections at the other three points. How is the answer related to the entries in $$D^{- 1}$$ ? [Hint: First answer the question when the deflection is $$1 \text{cm}$$ at the second point.]

problem.paragraph: $$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}A & I\end{matrix} \left]\right. & sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 & - 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ - 1 & 5 & 6 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & - 4 & 5 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 & - 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 10 & - 5 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 & - 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & - 7 & - 2 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

So $$\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix}$$ is row equivalent to a matrix of the form $$\begin{bmatrix} B & D \end{bmatrix}$$ , where $$B$$ is square and has a row of zeros. Further row operations will not transform $$B$$ into $$I$$ , so we stop. $$A$$ does not have an inverse.

Since $$A$$ is an invertible matrix, there exists a matrix $$C$$ such that $$AC = I = CA$$ . The goal is to find a matrix $$D$$ so that $$(5A)D = I = D(5A)$$ . Set $$D = 1/5C$$ . Applying Theorem 2 from Section 2.1 establishes that $$(5A)(1/5C) = \text{(5)(1/5)} (AC) = 1I = I$$ , and $$(1/5C) \text{(5} A) = \text{(1/5)} (5)(CA) = 1I = I$$ , Thus $$1 / 5$$ $$C$$ is indeed the inverse of $$A$$ , proving that $$A$$ is invertible.
